learning_objective: 🎯 Analyze and trace fundamental sorting algorithms — Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, and Insertion Sort — and evaluate their algorithmic efficiency.

key_vocabulary.definition: Arranging elements of a list or array in a specified logical order (ascending or descending).
A sorting algorithm that requires no extra memory space ($O(1)$ auxiliary space) and modifies the original list directly.
A measure of the computational time required by an algorithm as a function of the input size (N).

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After every full pass, the largest remaining element 'bubbles up' to its correct position at the end. Best case: $O(n)$ (optimized); Worst/Average case: $O(n^2)$.

Divides the list into a sorted left portion and an unsorted right portion. Repeatedly scans the unsorted portion to select the smallest element and swaps it with the first unsorted element. Always makes $O(n^2)$ comparisons regardless of initial order.

Works like sorting playing cards in your hand. Takes one element at a time from the unsorted section and shifts already-sorted elements right until it finds the correct insertion spot. Extremely efficient for small or nearly sorted lists ($O(n)$ best case).

exam_tips: 📌 In exam pass-tracing questions, show the state of the entire array after EACH complete pass of the outer loop — do not skip intermediate states.
📌 Selection Sort performs the minimum number of swaps ($O(n)$ swaps total) compared to Bubble Sort, making it preferable when writing to memory is expensive.
📌 An optimized Bubble Sort uses a `swapped = True/False` flag to break out early if the list becomes sorted before all passes finish.
quick_recap: ⭐ All three basic algorithms (Bubble, Selection, Insertion) have a worst-case time complexity of $O(n^2)$.
⭐ Insertion Sort is the algorithm used internally as a building block for advanced hybrid sorting engines (like Timsort in Python).
⭐ Bubble Sort is 'stable' (preserves the relative order of identical elements), whereas basic Selection Sort is generally 'unstable'.
